value.overview: The Highland Tinamou, also called Bonaparte’s Tinamou or Tinamú Serrano, is a secretive, ground-dwelling bird of humid mountain forests. It belongs to an ancient South American bird group that can fly but usually moves quietly through dense vegetation. The species is most often detected by its repeated whistle rather than seen. In Costa Rica, it is associated with highland and montane forests, including protected areas in the Cordillera de Guanacaste and other mountain ranges.
value.classification: The Highland Tinamou is a member of the tinamou family, Tinamidae, in the order Tinamiformes. The Costa Rican population is generally assigned to the subspecies Nothocercus bonapartei frantzii.
value.identification: This medium-sized tinamou measures about 38–41 cm long. It has a rounded body, short tail, gray legs, and a relatively small head. The back and wings are dark, mottled, or barred, with pale cream spotting. The breast is distinctly rufous or tawny, which helps separate it from the similar Great Tinamou. It is usually encountered walking on the forest floor, and its shy behavior, dark plumage, and dense habitat make visual identification difficult.
value.rangeHabitat: The species occurs from the highlands of Costa Rica and western Panama south through the Andes of Colombia, Venezuela, Ecuador, and northern Peru. In Costa Rica it is a resident of montane and humid highland forest, ranging from roughly 1,200 m to at least 2,500 m in suitable areas. Records include the Cacao sector of Área de Conservación Guanacaste. It favors wet, dense forest with a shaded, relatively open floor, thick undergrowth, and sometimes bamboo or other ground cover.
value.migrationStatus: Resident in Costa Rica and not considered a regular long-distance migrant. It is expected to remain in suitable highland forest throughout the year, although local movements may occur with food availability or weather.
value.breeding: Highland Tinamou breeding information is limited, but tinamous commonly nest on or very near the ground in sheltered vegetation or beside tree buttresses. The male generally incubates the eggs and cares for the young, while females may mate with more than one male. Reports for this species describe small clutches of glossy turquoise to violet eggs. Exact breeding dates in Costa Rica are not well documented, so the local nesting season should be treated as uncertain.
value.dietFeeding: It forages mainly on the forest floor, taking fallen fruits, seeds, and other plant material, along with insects and other small invertebrates. Feeding usually involves quiet walking and probing among leaf litter and low vegetation. Its diet may vary with seasonal fruiting and local forest conditions. Because it spends much of the day in dense cover, feeding activity is often heard or inferred from tracks and brief sightings rather than observed closely.
value.behavior: The Highland Tinamou is generally shy and difficult to observe. It usually walks rather than flies, but can make a rapid, explosive flight when startled. Individuals may forage alone or in loose association, and they retreat quickly when approached. Males give repeated, musical or tremulous whistles from their forest territories, especially during breeding activity. At night, the bird may roost on a low or moderate forest perch rather than sleeping on the ground.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not reliably quantified in commonly available summaries.
